ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This review involved no new data collection; the TMT-VR studies synthesised here were approved by the ethics committees named in their reports.
Within the two lineages, the older participants were mostly healthy or cognitively screened volunteers, and no assessment study included people with dementia.

The older TMT-VR participants were recruited through day centres for older adults (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026; Kourtesis et al., in press), and the Darts feasibility study took place at an elderly care centre (Goumopoulos et al., 2023).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Within the two lineages, the older participants were mostly healthy or cognitively screened volunteers, and no assessment study included people with dementia.

> The older TMT-VR participants were recruited through day centres for older adults (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026; Kourtesis et al., in press), and the Darts feasibility study took place at an elderly care centre (Goumopoulos et al., 2023).

> In the reports of the two later configurations, all participants completed both parts, no session was stopped for symptoms, and symptoms after headset removal were low (Table 2).

> In the selection-technique comparison, some volunteers were excluded after initial calibration failure, and the analysed sample comprised young and middle-aged adults (Kourtesis et al., 2025).

> Dome pilot (Plotnik et al., 2017) Sixteen volunteers were recruited and 11 analysed, after four calibration failures and one technical failure; Spearman 𝜌 .76 (A), .88 (B) and .59 (B-A, p = .056).

> Eye tracking and eyes-only mode (Wilf, Korakin et al., 2024) Thirty older adults and a five-person young group; paper-VR correlations are shown only in a figure; eye data of 3 participants were excluded for noisy tracking; errors could not be scored in the eyes-only mode.

Ethics approval statement:

> This review involved no new data collection; the TMT-VR studies synthesised here were approved by the ethics committees named in their reports.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1608 columns across 78 data files.
#### Issues Identified

4 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("SENS_P2_SocialSupport_Mode_Age_c130_v02.csv", "SENS_P2_Support_Education_c130_v02.csv", "matched_incremental_26.csv", "part_interactions.csv"), Column = c("warning", "warning", "high", "warnings"), Issues = c("⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 10 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 3 values are missing", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Values look like personal information: credit_card (1 value, 1%)", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 6 values are missing" )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding

2 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Respondent = c("37", "37"), "Blocks flagged" = c(1L, 
1L), Scales = c("acceptability (3-6, 10 items)", "acceptability (3-6, 10 items)"
), "Longest run" = c("same answer 8 times in a row, out of 10 items (flagged at 8)", 
"same answer 8 times in a row, out of 10 items (flagged at 8)"
), "Short-scale only" = c("no", "no")), row.names = 1:2, class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE)
```

**What this does not cover.** Only 2 of 78 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: This review involved no new data collection; the TMT-VR studies synthesised here were approved by the ethics committees named in their reports.
live_data_statements: Within the two lineages, the older participants were mostly healthy or cognitively screened volunteers, and no assessment study included people with dementia.

The older TMT-VR participants were recruited through day centres for older adults (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026; Kourtesis et al., in press), and the Darts feasibility study took place at an elderly care centre (Goumopoulos et al., 2023).
In the reports of the two later configurations, all participants completed both parts, no session was stopped for symptoms, and symptoms after headset removal were low (Table 2).
In the selection-technique comparison, some volunteers were excluded after initial calibration failure, and the analysed sample comprised young and middle-aged adults (Kourtesis et al., 2025).
Dome pilot (Plotnik et al., 2017) Sixteen volunteers were recruited and 11 analysed, after four calibration failures and one technical failure; Spearman 𝜌 .76 (A), .88 (B) and .59 (B-A, p = .056).

Eye tracking and eyes-only mode (Wilf, Korakin et al., 2024) Thirty older adults and a five-person young group; paper-VR correlations are shown only in a figure; eye data of 3 participants were excluded for noisy tracking; errors could not be scored in the eyes-only mode.

#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. info.title: Trail Making Tests in Extended Reality: A Critical Review with Implications for Cognitive Ageing

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								The American College of Greece
								
									153 42
									Athens
									Greece;

text.text: Extended reality (XR) versions of the Trail Making Test and Color Trails Test are promising for assessing and training cognition in older adults.
However, each XR adaptation is a new instrument, whose display, interaction technique, timing rules and layouts may change what it measures.
This critical narrative review maps these implementations by software lineage and appraises their evidence for assessment and training against common criteria.
The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), whose source code was inspected, serves as a measurement case.
XR trail-making tests showed convergence with paper and computerised versions, varying by test part and sample, and clinical group differences (e.g., Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment).

However, gaps in reliability (e.g., randomised forms), validation (e.g., norms, prospective samples) and reporting (e.g., error handling, build identity) emerged, and no training benefit attributable to the trail-making component was identified.
The TMT-VR case shows how interaction technique, timing rule, error handling and unlogged layouts shape a score's meaning.
Future tests should log layouts and events, estimate alternate-form reliability and undergo prospective validation, and training trials should isolate the trail-making component.
Several XR trail-making tests have moved beyond feasibility, and reported tolerability during supervised sessions supports further evaluation in older adults.
Cognitive assessment and cognitive training in older adults both need tasks that are interpretable, acceptable and accessible.
Immersive virtual reality (VR) is attractive for both purposes, because it adds experimental control, automated scoring and everyday-like content to a task (Parsons, 2015; Rizzo et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Immersive virtual reality (VR) is attractive for both purposes, because it adds experimental control, automated scoring and everyday-like content to a task <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Parsons, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Rizzo et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: However, every adaptation of a paper test is a new instrument, which needs its own reliability, validity, norms and technical documentation before a clinical claim is made (R. M. Bauer et al., 2012).
text.formatted: However, every adaptation of a paper test is a new instrument, which needs its own reliability, validity, norms and technical documentation before a clinical claim is made (R. M. <ref type="bibr">Bauer et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: It also needs software of adequate quality: suitable hardware, ergonomic interaction, tutorials, a steady frame rate and a measured symptom outcome (Kourtesis et al., 2019 (Kourtesis et al., , 2020;; Vlake et al., 2024).
text.formatted: It also needs software of adequate quality: suitable hardware, ergonomic interaction, tutorials, a steady frame rate and a measured symptom outcome <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Kourtesis et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Kourtesis et al., , 2020;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vlake et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The field has not yet met these standards in general.

Across 287 studies of VR neuropsychological testing, three tools * Correspondence: mailto:pkourtesis@acg.edu had normative data (Pieri et al., 2023), and across 24 studies of VR memory assessment, only one made its tasks openly accessible (Mancuso et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Across 287 studies of VR neuropsychological testing, three tools * Correspondence: <ref type="url" target="mailto:pkourtesis@acg.edu">pkourtesis@acg.edu</ref> had normative data <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Pieri et al., 2023)</ref>, and across 24 studies of VR memory assessment, only one made its tasks openly accessible <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Mancuso et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Older adults are not one group.

Healthy volunteers in their sixties, adults over 80, people with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia and care-home residents differ in vision, hearing, motor control, posture, fatigue and digital experience (Czaja et al., 2006; Schaumburg et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Healthy volunteers in their sixties, adults over 80, people with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia and care-home residents differ in vision, hearing, motor control, posture, fatigue and digital experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Czaja et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Schaumburg et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these characteristics can change a score or the willingness to continue.

Head-mounted VR has generally been accepted by older adults, symptoms have usually been minor, and empirically grounded design guidance exists (Arlati et al., 2021; Drazich et al., 2023; Huygelier et al., 2019; Ijaz et al., 2022; Vanden Abeele et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Head-mounted VR has generally been accepted by older adults, symptoms have usually been minor, and empirically grounded design guidance exists <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arlati et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Drazich et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Huygelier et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Ijaz et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Vanden Abeele et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, feasibility in young adults is not evidence for clinical ageing, and acceptability is not evidence of validity.
Training raises a further distinction.
Assessment validity shows that a task measures a construct; it does not show that practising the task improves cognition.
The evidence on VR training for MCI also comes from heterogeneous intervention packages, in which the contribution of any single task is hard to isolate (Qin et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025).

text.text: Trail making is a revealing case for these questions.

The geometry can change at every administration, which reduces the memorisation of a fixed form but adds a layout component to every score.
Finally, XR can provide timestamped records of selections, gaze and head pose, although these records are not implemented or reported consistently.
A paper examiner also records errors and times, so the potential gain is one of resolution, consistency and auditability (Wilf, Korakin et al., 2024).

text.text: This review asks what the evidence on XR trail-making tests supports for cognitive assessment and training, par-ticularly in older adults, and which design and measurement requirements remain unmet.
Eligibility is all-age, because much of the relevant work involves younger adults, and the limits of transfer to older and clinical groups are stated where they apply.
The review had three aims.
The first was to map and appraise the implementations by software lineage, applying the same criteria to each.
The second was to use the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), whose source code and study records were available for inspection, as a measurement case.
The third was to state what XR trail tests must demonstrate before clinical use or training claims, for readers in neuropsychology and in human-computer interaction (HCI).
Statements that a property was not found refer to the sources identified by this review (Section 2).
This is a critical narrative review with a structured evidence map, assembled from the project library and targeted supplementary searching.
It is not a systematic or scoping review.
The synthesis is narrative, because the question concerns design and evidence quality rather than a pooled effect.

Records were eligible for the XR inventory if they described a trail-making task delivered in head-mounted VR, head-mounted augmented or mixed reality (AR/MR), or a dome or large-screen immersive display.
A trailmaking task was defined as connecting targets in a prescribed sequence defined by numbers, letters, colours or their alternation, including the CTT and its relatives.
Assessment and training uses, any population, any publication type, any date and any language were eligible.
Conventional, desktop, tablet, walking, driving and screen-based eye-tracking trail tests were retained as contextual comparators and were not counted in the inventory.
A study that used a conventional TMT only as a comparator for immersive tasks of another kind was excluded (Davison et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A study that used a conventional TMT only as a comparator for immersive tasks of another kind was excluded <ref type="bibr">(Davison et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Studies in which a conventional TMT served only as the outcome of an XR intervention were classed as training evidence, unless the intervention itself contained a trail-making task.
The library was assembled by the author between September and 24 October 2026 from database searches and from the reference lists of held papers, using trailmaking, immersion and training terms.
The query strings and per-database counts were not logged, so the search cannot be reproduced as a database protocol.
Supplementary Section S1 reports it instead by its intakes, dates and record counts, with a reconciliation of the candidate records that a gap analysis identified.
The evidence map holds 152 records with 37 fields (File S1).
Of these, 144 were read in full text or in named sections, five only as abstracts or publisher records, two only by title and one only as a library note.
Records known only from an abstract were included at that level and are marked as such in the tables.
Screening and charting were performed by the author, and no second screener was involved.
Generative AI tools assisted with organising the literature records and with extracting and verifying their data, as detailed in the Acknowledgments.

Four units were kept distinct, because conflating them inflates the apparent evidence: the implementation lineage (related software from one group), the configuration (a version with its hardware, input, timing and language), the publication and the study.
Every implementation was appraised against the same criteria in five domains.
Reporting completeness used the RATE-XR items as reporting guidance and not as validation (Vlake et al., 2024).

Bauer et al., 2012), technical verification of timing, scoring, builds and layouts (Kourtesis et al., 2020; Parsons et al., 2018), and human factors and applicability to older adults and clinical groups (International Organization for Standardization, 2024; Zygouris & Tsolaki, 2015).

No compliance score was computed.

text.text: Posture ranges from standing, secured in the dome or free in a tracked area, to sitting on a fixed or swivel chair.
Selection ranges from reaching and touching, through a controller ray and button, to gaze or head orientation held on the target for a dwell.
Confirmation rules differ even within a lineage.

The eyes-only VR-CTT, for example, required a 100-ms fixation to select a correct target and a 500-ms fixation to select a wrong one, so that wrong selections were harder to complete (Wilf, Korakin et al., 2024).

text.text: Layouts are either fixed, as in the paper test, or newly generated, and either spread in depth or held at one distance.

The AR-TMT randomises target positions under spacing constraints and checked its arrangements by the mean head movement per target, which had a coefficient of variation of 7.7% across stages (Baek et al., 2025a).
text.formatted: The AR-TMT randomises target positions under spacing constraints and checked its arrangements by the mean head movement per target, which had a coefficient of variation of 7.7% across stages <ref type="bibr">(Baek et al., 2025a)</ref>.

text.text: Target fields also differ in angular extent.

The VR-CTT spreads its targets over about 120° horizontally, wider than the headset's field of view, and 52-62° vertically, so that head movement is part of the search (Lustig  , 2023; Wilf, Korakin et al., 2024).

text.text: The TMT-VR spans about 80° horizontally (Supplementary Section S6), whereas the epilepsy VR-TMT keeps all targets at one distance in the forward field, so that they share visual angle and selection conditions (Steininger et al., 2026).

text.text: Error handling also differs.
In the VR-CTT and the TMT-VR, wrong selections are registered and counted, and the participant continues from the last correct target.

In the epilepsy VR-TMT, the motion-capture CTT, the VR TMT-B game and the SoundShaping trail mode, a wrong selection does not advance the trail, and the participant must select the correct target (Adlakha et al., 2021; V. Bauer et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2026; Steininger et al., 2026).

text.text: The AR-TMT logs each selection as a hit or a miss without stating whether a miss advances the trail (Baek et al., 2025a).

text.text: The reports of the Darts game and the cancer-care TMT do not describe error handling.

A rule that stops a wrong selection from advancing the trail does not stop the selection itself, so completion times and error counts are not comparable across implementations unless each states whether wrong inputs are registered, counted, corrected or ignored.
These choices bear directly on older users.
Design guidance for immersive VR with older adults emphasises onboarding and assistance, practice, safe seating and multimodal feedback (Ijaz et al., 2022; Vanden Abeele et al., 2021).

text.text: In the empirically grounded set, first-use interviews gave no support to the advice to limit head movement or to avoid buttons and gestures, and some older adults found seated use limiting (Vanden Abeele et al., 2021).

text.text: This guidance says nothing about gaze or dwell selection, albeit one review notes that age-related decline of the vestibulo-ocular reflex may complicate gaze-based interaction (Schaumburg et al., 2025).

text.text: A design feature is therefore alignment with a recommendation, not evidence that the recommendation was met for intended users.
Head-gaze selection, for example, follows the advice to avoid buttons, whereas its head movement departs from the advice to limit head movement, and it places a demand on neck mobility.
Fitting is reported unevenly too.

Among the TMT-VR studies, one reports automatic interpupillary-distance adjustment (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026), and another reports that the examiner fitted the headset and adjusted the interpupillary distance (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026).

text.text: Depth deserves particular care.
It costs selection time in threedimensional pointing (Clark et al., 2020; Hou & Chen, 2021), and an incorrectly set interpupillary distance can impair depth perception (Schaumburg et al., 2025).

text.text: A test that uses depth therefore needs a characterised layout distribution and depth treated as a candidate difficulty factor.

In the residents' study, completion times improved across six sessions, mainly in the mirror-reversal segments, whereas regular segments stabilised after pre-shift practice (Gottlieb et al., 2027).

No retest or alternate-form estimate was identified for any randomised-layout XR trail test.
Clinical group evidence was reported for two lineages.

text.text: Age-group discrimination is not evidence of clinical accuracy.
No XR trail test was found to have normative data, a prospective validation in a referred clinical population or evidence of incremental value over an existing screening instrument.
Process measures are the most distinctive evidence of the VR-CTT lineage.

text.text: These older adults differed from a small young group in search duration and not in execution duration or velocity.

Head-hand lag lengthened from Part A to Part B and with age (Lustig et al., 2023), and patients with Parkinson's disease differed from controls in peak hand velocity and head-hand lag rather than in the share of search (Heimler et al., 2026).

text.text: These results show what continuous hand, head and gaze records can add to completion time.
They come from fixed layouts, and in the clinical study the discriminating variables were selected in the same sample without crossvalidation.
Error scores are less developed.
Patients with Parkinson's disease made more errors than controls in both formats (Heimler et al., 2026), and TMT-VR errors were age-related and separated adults with MCI (Table 2).

text.text: These results are human-factors evidence.
They show that a format was tolerated under supervision; they do not show that its scores measure the intended construct.
The training question has four levels, and the sources answer them unevenly (Table 3).

text.text: The first is whether XR training contains trail-like content and whether that content is acceptable.
One headset game does.

In the Darts game of the GAME2AWE platform, older adults burst numbered and lettered balloons in order by holding a central crosshair on each balloon until the arrow is released (Goumopoulos et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In the Darts game of the GAME2AWE platform, older adults burst numbered and lettered balloons in order by holding a central crosshair on each balloon until the arrow is released <ref type="bibr">(Goumopoulos et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Its feasibility study reported usability and symptoms for the platform as a whole and no performance data for any game.
By contrast, the trail-making mode of an AR music-making application is an embedded assessment of attention, not training content (V. Bauer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: By contrast, the trail-making mode of an AR music-making application is an embedded assessment of attention, not training content (V. <ref type="bibr">Bauer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The second level is whether programmes that contain such content change cognitive outcomes.
A pilot randomised trial of the GAME2AWE platform found exploratory improvements on both parts of the paper TMT against usual care (Goumopoulos et al., 2026).

text.text: The platform combined Kinect, smart-floor and VR games, the combination of games varied by session and difficulty adapted automatically.
The supplement that details the games was not accessible to this review, so exposure to the Darts game could not be verified.

text.text: These reviews overlap in their included trials and are not independent replications.
The third level is attribution.
No identified trial isolates the efficacy of an immersive trail-making component.
Immersion itself has not been isolated either.

A network meta-analysis gave larger point estimates for non-immersive and semi-immersive than for immersive interventions against attention control, albeit by comparing different packages rather than by manipulating immersion (Qin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: A network meta-analysis gave larger point estimates for non-immersive and semi-immersive than for immersive interventions against attention control, albeit by comparing different packages rather than by manipulating immersion <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Qin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The fourth level is transfer to outcomes that were not trained.
A gain on the paper TMT after practice on a traillike game would be near transfer within the trail-making family.
Broader benefit requires untrained measures of other cognitive functions and of everyday activity, with follow-up.
None of the identified studies combines an active comparator, a defined dose of trail-making content, untrained outcomes at both distances and follow-up.
Training software is also rarely shared (Navarro-Ramos et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Training software is also rarely shared <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Navarro-Ramos et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, head-mounted exergames have been feasible and tolerated by older adults when sessions were short, supervised and preceded by acclimatisation (Campo-Prieto et al., 2022; Goumopoulos et al., 2023; Parmak et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, head-mounted exergames have been feasible and tolerated by older adults when sessions were short, supervised and preceded by acclimatisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Campo-Prieto et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Goumopoulos et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Parmak et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The conditions for trials that can attribute a benefit to trail-making practice in XR are therefore in place.

text.text: The same criteria show that the implementations differ more in what they have tested than in what they report.
Most reports describe the display, task and selection method, but reporting remains incomplete for several implementations, most often for posture, error handling or build identity.
None reports a check of its completion times or error counts against an external clock or observer.
The samples are mostly convenience samples of young or healthy adults, and the clinical evidence comes from case-control designs.
Four gaps remain across the lineages, each bounded by the sources identified.
First, reliability rests on one lineage tested on a fixed layout.
Second, no implementation has normative data, a prospective validation in a referred population or a demonstrated increment over an existing screening instrument.
Third, depth and error handling differ between lineages and have not been isolated as sources of score variance.
No randomised-layout test has yet separated the search for a target from the movement to it.
Only the VR-CTT has validated such a segmentation, against manually scored eye-tracking video, although its authors note that the two components overlap (Wilf, Korakin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Only the VR-CTT has validated such a segmentation, against manually scored eye-tracking video, although its authors note that the two components overlap <ref type="bibr">(Wilf, Korakin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, code availability is uncommon.

The AR-TMT paper links a public repository (Baek et al., 2025a), the VR-CTT offers data on request, and the source code of the 2026 TMT-VR is released with this review under the MIT licence (Data Availability Statement).
text.formatted: The AR-TMT paper links a public repository <ref type="bibr">(Baek et al., 2025a)</ref>, the VR-CTT offers data on request, and the source code of the 2026 TMT-VR is released with this review under the MIT licence (Data Availability Statement).

text.text: A repository link does not by itself establish a licence, a deployable build or clinical readiness.
Applicability to older adults rests on two lineages.
Among the implementations with validation data, only the VR-CTT and the TMT-VR have evaluated adults over 65, and only the TMT-VR has evaluated older adults with MCI.
The AR-TMT, the motion-capture CTT and the epilepsy VR-TMT have been evaluated in young or middle-aged adults.
Within the two lineages, the older participants were mostly healthy or cognitively screened volunteers, and no assessment study included people with dementia.

The older TMT-VR participants were recruited through day centres for older adults (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026; Kourtesis et al., in press), and the Darts feasibility study took place at an elderly care centre (Goumopoulos et al., 2023).

text.text: The olderadult evidence therefore covers the healthier part of the population that these tests are meant to serve.
The fixed-layout tests cannot answer the reliability question for randomised forms, and the randomisedlayout tests have not yet reported reliability.

text.text: The current version selects by head-gaze: a reticle at the centre of view registers a target after a continuous 0.5-s dwell, and the dwell restarts if the reticle leaves the target.
The dwell duration was set during the development of this version, after a pilot in 12 young and middle-aged adults.
In that pilot 0.5 s performed better than longer durations on the System Usability Scale, which was the main criterion, and in oral feedback on the complexity of the task and on fatigue.
The reports of the first configuration give the dwell as 2 s or 1.5 s.
The 2024 and 2025 project files set the confirmation time to 0.5 s on every target handler, with the restart on exit.
The published descriptions of the 2024-2025 studies are those of the papers, and the build each of those studies used was not archived with its data.
The versions are therefore presented as distinct.
The configurations also differ in ways that change scores.
The first two timed a part from its activation to the 25th selection, whereas the current version times from the first confirmation to the 25th, so that 24 links are timed.

B-A is therefore not age-neutral, and the null for B/A does not show that B/A is.

text.text: The paper Part A separated the groups (g = 0.57, .14 to 1.00), albeit with an uncertain difference between formats (ΔAUC -.121, -.276 to .033; p = .125).
The lower manual demand of head-gaze selection is one possible explanation among the differences between formats.
Point estimates of discrimination favoured the TMT-VR's error and Part B-derived scores, although no difference between formats survived correction across 22 paired comparisons.
The Mini-Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination (M-ACE) discriminated better than any single score.

Given an education difference of four years, an asymmetric reference standard and no reliability estimate, the TMT-VR remains a candidate trail-making format for MCI neuropsychological batteries pending prospective validation.
Convergence held for time scores and not for error counts.

Within the English age groups, the Part B time correlation survived correction in both the younger (.43; Holm p = .024) and the older group (.48; Holm p = .010), and the Part A and B-A correlations did not (Kourtesis, O'Connor & MacPherson, 2026b).

text.text: Error counts did not converge.
The paper examiner corrects each error as it occurs, whereas the application registers every completed dwell on a wrong target.
In the MCI comparison, the observed maxima were 4 errors on paper and 22 in VR (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In the MCI comparison, the observed maxima were 4 errors on paper and 22 in VR <ref type="bibr">(Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The differing recording rules may contribute to the lack of convergence.

Ratios of group means between head-gaze and paper times were about 3.0 for Part A in the healthy groups and 2.6 in MCI, and 1.5-2.1 for Part B (Kourtesis, Ioakeimidou et al., 2026; Kourtesis, O'Connor & MacPherson, 2026b).

text.text: They are not individual ratios or conversion factors, and paper norms do not transfer to the TMT-VR.
Source inspection explains part of these patterns.
Each of the 24 timed links includes a nominal 0.5-s confirmation, which adds a nominal 12 s to each part, and an interrupted dwell adds time that is not logged.
A wrong-target error is a completed dwell on an unselected target other than the next target in the sequence.
It is counted from the start of the part, so the counting window begins before the clock.
A pause on a wrong target during search therefore completes a selection, and the error count can combine sequence errors with interactionrelated selections.
Error-adjusted time, the completion time multiplied by (1 + errors/24), depends on both.
The record has a larger gap.
Every run generates a new layout, and no layout was stored.
Path length varies between layouts with a coefficient of variation of about 10%, so each score contains a layout component of unknown size (Supplementary Section S6).
The examined placement routine also used the candidate field unevenly, favouring the nearest and farthest depth planes.
It shuffles with a sort that uses a random comparison, which violates the sort's contract and occasionally leaves a part without targets.
Neither layouts nor such failures were logged, so whether any past session met the defect cannot be established, although a part without targets would have been visible to the examiner.
Layouts are independent of age by construction, so additive, age-independent layout effects add variance to age associations rather than bias.
Because the layouts of the two parts are drawn independently, B-A carries the layout variance of both parts.
By contrast, the nominal dwell contribution cancels from B-A and not from B/A.

Design A reproducible XR trail test must record each run's layout and seed, an event log of timestamped target entries, exits, interrupted dwells and completions, a head-pose log, and a session manifest that identifies the build, configuration and language.
Scores can then be recomputed from events, the clock checked against an external clock, and the layout component of a score measured.
For the TMT-VR, a seeded repair of the placement routine, these logging components and a bank of 4,000 candidate forms had been written and checked outside the Unity Editor.
These components had not been integrated into the application or tested in the Unity Editor or on a headset as of 26 October 2026 (Supplementary Section S5).
The repair is designed to reproduce every placement from a logged seed, including recovery from the sort failure.
It did so for every tested seed in emulation, which remains to be shown on the deployed backend.
The candidate forms were matched on path length, summed angular separation and a Fitts-type index.

Their coefficients of variation on these summaries are below 1%, against 10%, 13% and 5% among fresh layouts, although selection shifted other properties, such as vertical extent and the share of far targets (Supplementary Section S6).
Geometric matching therefore reduces variation in the matched summaries, albeit without establishing equivalent difficulty for participants, alternate-form reliability or retest reliability.
Fresh layouts and bank forms are two administration distributions and need distinct configuration identities.
Recorded form histories, with verified exclusion of forms already seen, would reduce re-exposure to a specific path, although procedural, strategy and expectancy effects would remain.

Such records would allow a retest and alternate-form study that estimates reliability and the variation due to persons, sessions and forms, and that evaluates differences between forms against prespecified equivalence margins.
Interaction design is the second implication.
As currently exported, neither the paper TMT nor the head-gaze TMT-VR separates the time spent finding the next target from the time spent reaching and confirming it.

A computer-administered TMT has separated search from movement, with age effects on both (Salthouse & Fristoe, 1995), and eye and hand trajectories on a screen index separable processes (Juantorena et al., 2024; Linari et al., 2022).

Psychomotor performance is itself relevant to cognitive ageing, as age differences in simple and choice reaction times illustrate (Deary et al., 2011).

text.text: Controller ray-casting adds a manual component absent from head-gaze selection, although it does not reproduce pencil tracing.
Ray-casting is the candidate because the targets lie beyond reach and direct touch showed the steepest proportional age slope (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026).

text.text: Continuous head and controller logs could therefore serve two aims.
They could retain psychomotor performance that may be informative in its own right, and help examine how movement execution and cognitive control contribute to the score, especially in Part A.
The logs would relate movement paths, target visits and interrupted dwells to completion time.
Where the final uninterrupted entry into a target is recorded, the interval before that entry can be distinguished from the confirmation interval that follows it.
These intervals are operational.
The first still combines search, decision and movement, and movement itself involves planning and online correction.
Head orientation is not gaze, and neither interval measures pure motor speed.
Validated segmentation, reliability estimates and a suitable motor baseline would be needed to investigate their contributions.
A resulting motor index could first be examined alongside completion time and as a covariate, without assuming that adjustment leaves a pure cognitive score.
Whether these records clarify age and clinical-group differences in Part A is the empirical question, and its answer would inform both assessment and the design of training tasks.
The evidence reviewed here shows XR trail-making tests to be promising instruments, albeit with partial evidence for any clinical or training use.
The TMT-VR case adds that the interaction technique, the confirmation and timing rules, the error definition and the layout record shape what such scores mean.
For neuropsychologists, the requirements before clinical use are the familiar ones, applied to a new instrument (R. M. Bauer et al., 2012).
text.formatted: For neuropsychologists, the requirements before clinical use are the familiar ones, applied to a new instrument (R. M. <ref type="bibr">Bauer et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Reliability must be estimated on the forms actually administered, which for randomised layouts means retest and alternate-form designs (Zygouris & Tsolaki, 2015).
text.formatted: Reliability must be estimated on the forms actually administered, which for randomised layouts means retest and alternate-form designs <ref type="bibr">(Zygouris & Tsolaki, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Scores need their own norms from prospective stratified samples.
Diagnostic accuracy needs prospective validation in referred populations, with the reference standard applied to everyone and the increment over existing screening instruments tested.
Error scores need definitions that separate sequence errors from interactionrelated selections before they can support clinical decisions.
Performance validity needs either a validated built-in indicator or a recommendation of concurrent validated measures (R. M. Bauer et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Performance validity needs either a validated built-in indicator or a recommendation of concurrent validated measures (R. M. <ref type="bibr">Bauer et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Samples should also reach the older adults these tests are meant for, including adults over 80, people with MCI or dementia, care-home residents and people with sensory or motor impairment, with education sampled broadly.
For HCI researchers, the field and the case point to what should be logged, verified and reported.
Every study should state a configuration identity: device, build, input and confirmation rule, timing boundary, posture and language.
The layout of every run and an event log should be stored, and the error rule should state whether wrong inputs are registered, counted, corrected or ignored.
Timing should be verified against an external clock, and symptoms should be measured with their time window stated, inside the headset as well as after removal where possible.
Interaction choices change what is measured in older users.
Head-gaze dwell avoids buttons, albeit at the cost of neck movement and of wrong selections completed by pauses during search.
A controller ray adds manual coordination, direct touch showed the steepest relative age slope, and depth adds selection time.
These choices are therefore part of the construct and should be tested with intended users rather than settled by convention.
The trail-making loop is also a candidate training mechanic.
Each link requires a search under a rule, the inhibition of distractors, a movement and a confirmation, and Part B adds a switch between rules.
These demands are cognitive and motor at once, which suits exergames for older adults but complicates attribution.
One concept that follows is a seated game in which players release laser or water pistols at balloons or similar targets in sequence.
Such a game would need the evidence that Section 3.3 found missing, and its design should begin with intended users.
A seated exergame for persons living with dementia, for example, used no buttons and a recorded therapist voice as a guide (Muñoz et al., 2022).
text.formatted: A seated exergame for persons living with dementia, for example, used no buttons and a recorded therapist voice as a guide <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Muñoz et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: That precedent supports button-free interaction with guidance; it does not establish a universal input rule.
Trigger confirmation and drifting targets are therefore candidate choices to be tested.
The available Fitts data cannot show that a trigger is faster than dwell for older adults, because every mode in them used dwell (Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The available Fitts data cannot show that a trigger is faster than dwell for older adults, because every mode in them used dwell <ref type="bibr">(Kourtesis, Denaxa, Asimakopoulou et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Moving targets carry known costs as well.
In one co-designed exergame, approaching targets were replaced with static ones after older participants found their pacing difficult (Shah et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In one co-designed exergame, approaching targets were replaced with static ones after older participants found their pacing difficult <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Shah et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In another, adults around 80 caught fewer targets in a headset than in a projection-based room, although the headset gave greater presence (Karaosmanoglu et al., 2025).

text.text: The nearest precedent for the mechanic, a seated sword game with Stroop rules, was played by 12 older adults for 20 supervised sessions without a control arm (Du et al., 2024).

text.text: Dose needs descriptors that can be reported and replicated: the amount and range of movement, its intensity and the session duration, rather than duration and perceived exertion alone.
The training game and the assessment should also remain separate configurations.
A game may adapt spacing, tempo and difficulty, whereas the assessment keeps its rules and configuration identity, so that a change after training is not confounded with a change to the instrument.
A comparator, untrained outcomes and follow-up are required.
Gains on paper or VR trail tests after trail-like practice should be expected as near transfer, unless a broader outcome is justified in advance.
Adaptive difficulty raises a further question.
In the English assessment cohort, ratings of the experience were not associated with performance (Kourtesis, O'Connor & MacPherson, 2026a).
text.formatted: In the English assessment cohort, ratings of the experience were not associated with performance <ref type="bibr">(Kourtesis, O'Connor & MacPherson, 2026a)</ref>.

text.text: Such cross-sectional nulls justify neither including nor excluding frustration as an input to adaptation, which needs training-specific evidence.
Colour is a design question too.

Colour rules and feedback should be tested for discrimination and legibility with intended players, including older adults with cognitive impairment and people with colour-vision deficiencies, on the actual display.
An immersive trailmaking game is therefore a testable proposal, and trials that isolate its contribution will decide its value.
Overall, XR can make trail making more controlled, more richly recorded and more engaging for older adults.
These advantages become evidence when the configuration is reported, the record is complete and each claim is tested in the population and design it concerns.
This review applies the same criteria to every implementation and keeps lineages, configurations and studies apart.
Its case rests on inspected source code and project records rather than on published descriptions alone.
Its limitations indicate five directions for future work.

First, one author screened and charted the records, without duplicate screening or logged queries, so implementations may have been missed; a registered scoping review with logged searches and duplicate screening should follow.
Second, several sources were available only as abstracts or records, including several implementation reports, a trial supplement and a recent preprint attributed to the VR-CTT lineage.
Obtaining them could change the inventory and the training appraisal.

Third, the implementations differ in display, selection, layout, error handling and population, so the comparisons are qualitative; a common reporting set for XR trail tests would make them comparable.
Fourth, the author developed the TMT-VR, so its appraisal is a self-appraisal under common criteria, and an independent appraisal of the software is needed.

Fifth, the build used in some studies was not archived with their data, so the link between a study and an examined build rests partly on project records; future studies should archive the build with the data.
Trail making in XR has moved beyond feasibility, albeit not yet to clinical use.

Convergent associations with paper or computerised trail tests were reported for four implementations, retest reliability for one lineage on a fixed layout and clinical group differences for two lineages.
Normative data, prospective clinical validation, reliability of randomised forms and training benefit attributable to an immersive trail-making component were not identified.
The TMT-VR case shows why these gaps matter: the interaction technique, the confirmation and timing rules, the error definition and unlogged random layouts all shape the meaning of a score.

Further development for assessment therefore requires reported configurations, logged layouts and events, reliability estimated on the forms administered and prospective validation in the populations targeted.
Training claims also require trials that isolate the trail-making component and test untrained outcomes.
Overall, older adults, including adults with MCI, have tolerated supervised XR trail-making sessions well, which makes these next steps feasible.

text.text: Formula inspection is not an executed scoring test, and compile checks with lifecycle stubs are not runtime tests.

The selector documents a repeat risk of about 0.4% without exclusions and a fallback when every form of a pool has been excluded; recorded form histories with verified exclusion would reduce re-exposure to a specific path without eliminating it.
Geometry.
Each part presents 25 white cubes of 0.25-m edge, labelled on all six faces, in a plain room, with no distractors.
The first target is fixed 3 m ahead and about 15° above eye level and serves as the start marker.
The other 24 are placed one at a time from 167 candidate positions on six frontal planes 3-8 m away.
Each plane is a 7 × 4 grid at 1-m pitch, raised by 0.5 m and offset laterally relative to the one before it.
A layout spans about 80° horizontally and from 4° below to 43° above eye level, and a cube subtends about 4.8° at 3 m and 1.8° at 8 m.

At each step the routine shuffles six regions of the field and six distance bands (1-1.99 m to 6-6.99 m from the previous target), takes the first combination that holds an unused candidate, and draws one candidate from it at random.
Every start of a part produces a new layout, which the 2026 version does not store.

Ten thousand emulated layouts per part and 6,000 attempted layouts per part generated in Unity (5,998 and 5,999 produced) agreed on every summary but one (Kolmogorov-Smirnov D ≤ .017, except the vertical extent of Part A, D = .026).

Placement shares by plane, from 3 m to 8 m, were 39%, 1%, 12%, 1%, 7% and 40%; this non-uniform use of the field is an observed property of the examined routine, and no comparison has isolated its cause.
Geometric path length was 87.1 m (SD 8.9; coefficient of variation 10%; 5th-95th percentiles 72.6-101.8 m).

The summed angular separation between successive targets at the 1.20-m reference eye position was 506° (SD 68; coefficient of variation 13%; 398-622°); it is a geometric demand, not a recorded head rotation.

A Fitts-type geometric index summed over the 24 links was 75.0 bits (SD 3.6; coefficient of variation 5%; 69.0-80.8); it has not been related to participant performance and is not a calibrated difficulty scale.
Depth-plane changes were 15.9 of 24 (SD 2.4).
The mean target distance was 6.43 m, and 46% of targets lay at 7-8 m.
Under a conservative criterion, 0.8 targets per layout were partly hidden from the seat (0.2 after a 0.3-m lean), and 81% of layouts were free of occlusion after the lean.
Practice and test layouts were uncorrelated on every summary (r -.01 to +.02), as were Parts A and B (r +.01).
Modelled contribution of layouts.

Under the assumption that completion time is proportional to path length, simulated layout dispersion would account for about 11% of the completion-time variance in early adulthood, 4% in middle and late adulthood and 2% across the lifespan sample, with per-part shares of 14-16% and 6-7% (Kourtesis et al., in press).

text.text: These are sensitivity calculations under stated assumptions; the contribution of the layouts actually encountered remains unmeasured.

Layouts are independent of age by construction, so additive, age-independent layout effects add variance rather than bias; age-dependent sensitivity to geometry cannot be excluded without logged Placement defect.
The shuffle is the .
NET list sort with a random comparer, which violates the contract of the sort, so the sort occasionally throws an exception and the part then has no targets.

In an exact emulation run with Unity's Mono class library, the exception occurred in 366 of 10 6 Part A placements and 374 of 10 6 Part B placements of test size, and in 86 of 10 6 tutorial-size placements.

Under the assumptions of independence and representativeness used in the calculation, the two recorded test placements of a session give a probability of .00074 of meeting the exception (about one session in 1,352), and the probability that at least one of 230 sessions met it is .16.
Counting the two tutorial and two practice placements as well, the figures are .0017 (about one session in 606) and .32.
These are model-based probabilities, not observed failure rates.
Because neither layouts nor exceptions were logged, the study records cannot establish whether a past session encountered this placement exception.
Candidate form bank.
The bank holds 4,000 distinct layouts in four pools of 1,000 (practice A, test A, practice B, test B), selected from fresh layouts of the seeded repair by frozen criteria.

Every form lies within ±0.10 SD of the pilot medians on path length (87.21 ± 0.90 m), summed angular separation (503.9 ± 6.8°) and the Fitts-type index (74.99 ± 0.36 bits), has 16 ± 1 depth-plane changes and horizontal and vertical extents within ±0.5 SD, and shows no substantial overlap under an inscribed-sphere approximation at eye heights of 1.10, 1.20, 1.30 and 1.36 m.
An independent recalculation confirmed that all 4,000 forms meet these criteria.
Within the bank, the coefficients of variation are 0.60% for path length, 0.77% for angular separation and 0.27% for the index, against 10%, 13% and 5% among fresh layouts.

Selection shifts other properties: the mean vertical extent is 45.98° against 42.6° among fresh layouts (+8%), and the share of far targets still varies between forms (coefficient of variation 12.5%; range .28-.64).
Matching on three summaries reduces variation in those summaries.

It does not establish equivalent difficulty for participants, alternate-form reliability or retest reliability, and it does not remove differences in visual search, target order or neck movement between forms.
Reproduction of a placement from its seed has been shown for the tested seeds in emulation only.

text.text: The Methods name Kruskal-Wallis tests for form and order and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for the A/B comparison, which, as reported, do not account for repeated observations of the same people.
There was no control condition repeating one form, so reduced practice effects cannot be shown.
The power rationale concerned the A/B difference.
The abstract states a significant A/B difference for every form, whereas only forms 1, 2 and 5 meet the stated alpha of .02.
The paper-VR correlations use each person's average across the five forms (𝜌 .68 for A; .51 for B, p = .05, not significant at alpha .02), and individual-form coefficients vary.
